title: The coachee continuum: how coachable are you?
author: Thahmina Begum
summary: Thahmina Begum, writing for staff at Community Schools Trust where live, in-the-moment coaching is standard practice, argues that live coaching's success depends as much on how the teacher being coached receives it as on how the coach delivers it. Citing Ryan Holiday's distinction between "alive time" (actively using time well) and "dead time," she frames live coaching as a way of making classroom moments alive time through incremental, in-the-moment improvement, but notes her school has invested heavily in training coaches while giving little attention to training the coachee side of the exchange. Using a "coachee continuum" built by a colleague, Begum shows that defensive or dismissive responses to live coaching fail both stated success criteria -- that it look like team teaching to students and that the coached teacher feel the coach is invested in their development -- regardless of whether the feedback itself was actually good. She offers three concrete scripts for receiving live coaching well: casually agreeing and adopting the suggestion mid-lesson, turning the moment into a question that draws on the coach's subject expertise, and jokingly feigning shared surprise at a lapse before correcting it -- all framed as ways to preserve the appearance of team teaching to students while genuinely incorporating the feedback. She closes by arguing that coachability, not just coaching skill, determines whether the technique actually works, since a defensive reaction undermines the process even when the underlying feedback was sound.
points: Begum's central claim: live coaching's two success criteria (looking like team teaching to students, and the coachee feeling the coach is invested in their growth) depend as much on the coachee's response as on the coach's delivery.
She notes a specific training gap at her school: extensive training exists for coaches, but almost none for how teachers should receive live coaching -- despite live coaching depending on both sides.

Her three scripted responses -- casual agreement, turning the moment into a question for the coach, and jokingly feigning shared surprise -- are all designed to preserve the appearance of team teaching to students while genuinely adopting the feedback.

Begum argues that even objectively rubbish feedback is better served by a coachable response than a defensive one, since defensiveness fails both success criteria regardless of whether the original feedback was any good.
quotes: Live coaching is one way we make our time ‘alive time’ – stepping in, in the moment, in order to slightly improve our craft, perfectly captures the idea of actively using time usefully.
It occurred to me though, we haven’t given a lot of attention to how we RECEIVE live coaching.
The response examples on the continuum clearly indicate that the live coaching has not been successful. Neither of the two criteria have been fulfilled.
As much as it is the coach's responsibility to fulfil the criteria of effective feedback, so too is it the coachee's.
Your ego screams for people to acknowledge you. But you must do nothing. Take it. Eat it until you’re sick. Endure it.
Be coachable. Make your time ‘alive time’. Be on the right side of the coachee continuum.
